name: Anti-wrinkle pillow
lead: Anti-wrinkle pillows are contoured, cut-out or cushioned pillows, and smooth pillowcases made of silk, satin or similar fabrics, sold to reduce pressure and creasing of the face against bedding during sleep. People use them to keep the forehead, cheeks and chest from picking up lines while they sleep, aiming for smoother-looking skin over the years.[3]

The premise is that sleep wrinkles form when the face is pressed, stretched and compressed against a pillow, particularly in side and stomach sleepers. Researchers at the University of Queensland writing in The Conversation describe sleep wrinkles as creases that usually fade soon after waking in younger skin but can become lasting lines as skin loses elasticity, and note that people who always sleep on one side often show more lines on that side.[3] Wikipedia lists habitual sleeping position among the factors that can contribute to skin wrinkling, alongside ageing, sun damage, smoking, weight loss and facial expressions.[1]

The same Conversation article says pillows designed to reduce mechanical stress on the face may help limit skin deformation in sleep, and that smooth fabrics such as silk may help if they let skin glide rather than drag.[3] No published clinical trial of anti-wrinkle pillow products was located, so product claims rest on this mechanical theory and manufacturer descriptions.

chain: Pillow shape or smooth cover reduces pressure and drag on the face
Less repeated creasing in the same facial areas
Fewer or fainter sleep lines over time
angle.text: Users buy these pillows to cut nightly compression of the face, expecting sleep lines on the cheeks, forehead and chest to be shallower. The routine works alongside other approaches commonly described for wrinkles, such as sunscreen and moisturizing.[3]

infobox: Contoured pillow or smooth pillowcase intended to reduce facial compression
Less facial pressure and shear; lower friction for silk-type covers[3]
Sleeping on the back or changing positions[3]

paras: Designs include pillows with cut-outs or channels that let the cheek or forehead rest without contact, cradle-shaped or wedge pillows that encourage back sleeping, and flat pillowcases of silk, satin or copper-infused fabric intended to let skin glide. Pillows in general are bedding items designed for head and neck support and comfort, in varied shapes, sizes and fillings.[2]

The Queensland authors say pressing the face into a pillow stretches, compresses and pulls the skin, especially for side and stomach sleepers, because gravity pushes the face into the pillow and movement during sleep pulls the skin in several directions.[3] They say the pattern and rate of line formation depend on how long each position is held, the force on each part of the face and how much of the face touches the pillow.[3]

Wikipedia describes the misrepair-accumulation theory of ageing, in which wrinkles develop from incorrect repair of elastic and collagen fibres injured by repeated extension and compression of the skin, and lists repeated facial expressions and frequent sleeping positions among contributors.[1] Proponents of anti-wrinkle pillows apply this idea to hours of nightly facial compression.[3] The Conversation article adds that ageing reduces skin's recoil and stretch, which lets temporary creases become persistent.[3]

The same article lists sleeping on the back or changing positions overnight, moisturizing before bed, ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, and general measures such as sun protection, not smoking, hydration and a healthy diet.[3] It explains that moisturisers work through occlusive ingredients that reduce water loss and humectants that attract water.[3] Wikipedia lists sun exposure, smoking, dehydration and ageing as promoters of wrinkling and describes clinical options including tretinoin and tazarotene, fillers, botulinum toxin and lasers, which act on wrinkles by different routes than pillows do.[1]

Pillows in general are bedding items designed for head and neck support and comfort, in varied shapes, sizes and fillings.[2] Pillows and pillowcases marketed specifically against sleep lines belong to the broader beauty-sleep product category, which includes silk and satin cases, copper-infused fabrics and shaped cushions. Sleep wrinkles drew wider attention in 2023 to 2024 when University of Queensland researchers described them in The Conversation, and the article was shared on Hacker News in 2024.[3][4]

No studies found of anti-wrinkle pillows or silk pillowcases for wrinkle outcomes. The Queensland authors say studies they cite show that pillows designed to reduce mechanical stress during sleep can prevent skin deformations, and that such a pillow could be useful in slowing or preventing certain facial wrinkles; they describe this as a possibility rather than a demonstrated result.[3]
Risks are low. Reported downsides are discomfort or disturbed sleep from an unfamiliar shape, and cost.

Within skin-care and appearance communities, sleeping position is discussed as a cause of facial lines, with back sleeping suggested as a no-cost alternative to specialised pillows. The Conversation article was also posted to Hacker News in 2024 under the title 'Sleep Wrinkles Are Real'.[3][4] Specialised pillows and silk cases are commonly priced from roughly $40 to $100.

lore.intro: Sleep position and pillow type come up in skin-care and appearance discussion as a free or low-cost way to avoid facial lines; the topic was posted on Hacker News in 2024.[3][4]

claims.claim: Sleeping on one side or your stomach creates lasting wrinkles on that side of the face.
claims.believers: Skin-care writers and some dermatology practitioners describe flatter faces and more visible lines on a person's preferred side.[3]
claims.experts: The Queensland authors say sleep wrinkles are temporary in younger skin but can set in with age, and that skin specialists can often recognise the one-sided pattern.[3]

claims.claim: Silk pillowcases or contoured pillows prevent sleep wrinkles.
claims.believers: Users buy them expecting that skin will glide and face pressure will be reduced.[3]
claims.experts: The Conversation authors say silk may help if it lets skin glide and that stress-reducing pillows could be useful; no trial of these products for wrinkle outcomes was found.[3]
